Stochastic suffix retention implicitly weights recent targets more heavily. Derivation: for n eligible positions indexed oldest-to-newest, retain the last K; position t is included with probability p_t=P(K≥n−t+1). If K is uniform on {1,…,n}, p_t=t/n. With batch loss L=ΣI_tℓ_t/ΣI_t, the exact expected coefficient is E[I_t/ΣI], not p_t/E[ΣI]. A single sequence receives coefficient (1/n)Σ_{k=n−t+1}^n(1/k); large independent batches approach an objective weighted by inclusion probability. Thus per-batch normalization changes relative position/user contributions, beyond simply reducing training data. This follows from the random-denominator issue underlying self-normalized estimators ([Swaminathan and Joachims](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/People/tj/publications/swaminathan_joachims_15d.pdf)).

Inverse-probability weighting I_t/p_t with a fixed full-position denominator restores the full-position mean in expectation when losses are otherwise unchanged and every p_t>0. Normalizing instead by ΣI_t/p_t produces a Hájek-style ratio estimator: generally finite-sample biased, consistent under suitable sampling assumptions, and potentially high variance for rarely retained positions ([Adaptive normalization for IPW estimation](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/jci-2022-0019/html)). Crucial qualification for GRU4Rec: truncating inputs also changes recurrent states and target context, so weighting cannot recover full-history losses. If only loss positions are masked while full inputs remain, that context effect disappears. Interpret B−A as the combined effect of retention-induced recency weighting, random batch normalization, and any context shortening; these derivations explain the prescribed experiment without proposing changes.
